paragraphs: This checklist is for self-reflection only. It is not a hiring standard, ability score, or assessment of food safety. This page follows the U.S. O*NET-SOC 35-2021.00 occupation, Food Preparation Workers (the fixed index assigns this asset the Chinese name meaning Food Preparation Workers; its main scope is performing various food preparation duties other than cooking, such as preparing cold foods and shellfish, slicing meat, and brewing coffee or tea).

Practice scenario | An entirely fictional canteen needs to prepare a batch of cold foods and side dishes for service. Draft preparation and hygiene records explaining: (1) how to check ingredient names, quantities, and condition against orders or instructions and check storage temperatures; (2) how to wash, peel, slice, and cut ingredients with manual or powered utensils; (3) how to prepare cold foods, salads, and beverages using approved procedures, then portion, package, and plate them; (4) how to record ingredient usage and refrigerator and freezer temperatures and identify abnormalities; (5) how to clean and sanitize work areas, equipment, and tableware before and after work and report equipment faults or abnormal ingredients. Answer using public information and simulated data, without any real company, product, or customer information.

Fit signals | O*NET highlights working indoors in an environmentally controlled setting daily (88%), wearing common protective or safety equipment daily (74%), constant contact with others (42%), daily face-to-face discussions with individuals and teams (62%), daily telephone communication (46%), the importance of repeating the same tasks (47% rate it extremely important), the importance of exactness or accuracy (46% rate it extremely important), standing more than half the time (36%), walking or running more than half the time (35%), and using hands more than half the time (34%). If you are willing to follow procedures for washing, cutting, portioning, and hygiene while maintaining a steady pace, this occupation's everyday demands may align more closely with your working style.

Caution signals | O*NET also reports daily time pressure (36%), continual or almost continual repetitive motions (17%), high responsibility for others' health and safety (25%), and serious consequences of error (65% consider them serious), because errors involving food safety, allergens, and hygiene directly affect others' health. The work involves cuts from knives, slicers, and grinders; slippery floors; burns from hot beverages and foods; and prolonged standing and walking. If you find sustained standing, repetitive washing and cutting, or remaining sufficiently alert to food safety and hygiene demands difficult, treat these as practical costs requiring careful consideration.

Assessing responsibility | Real fit depends on whether you can do three things within the same shift: prepare food correctly by following procedures (check, wash, and cut ingredients; prepare cold foods and drinks to order; portion and plate); maintain food safety and hygiene (hand and utensil hygiene, separation of raw and cooked foods, temperature records, and retained samples); and maintain records that can be checked (ingredient usage, refrigerator and freezer temperatures, and reports of equipment faults and abnormal ingredients). Test this through a verifiable experience, such as observing or helping in a canteen or kitchen, completing food safety and hygiene training with a practical assessment, or undertaking a simulated preparation and hygiene exercise, rather than relying solely on an interest questionnaire.

Safe work sample (an entirely fictional task package): Given a simulated cold-food and side-dish preparation list with one salad, one cold platter, two beverages, an allergen warning, and refrigeration temperature requirements, spend 60 minutes drafting preparation and hygiene records. Include ingredient checks (names, quantities, condition, and shelf life), a washing and cutting plan (utensils and sequence), a preparation and portioning plan (orders or instructions, portions, and plating), hygiene and sanitizing procedures (hands, utensils, and worktops), temperature and storage records (refrigerator and freezer readings), and abnormality handling and reporting procedures. Specify situations requiring work to stop and be reported rather than handled independently, such as spoiled ingredients, temperatures outside limits, equipment faults, and allergen contamination.

Scope and boundaries | O*NET-SOC35-2021.00 centers on food preparation and kitchen assistance. O*NET tasks include dishwashing, beverage service, limited cooking, and taking payments; an overlapping task alone does not change the occupational classification. Cooks, dishwashers, and front-counter workers are distinguished by their main duties. Authorization for statutory inspections, food safety incident determinations, and repairs must be checked separately.

Work context | O*NET 35-2021.00 work-context data show that work mainly involves food preparation and cleaning, usually indoors in controlled environments; conditions vary by business type and site.
Environment | Work indoors in an environmentally controlled setting daily (88%).
Protective equipment | Wear common protective or safety equipment daily (74%), including gloves, aprons, and slip-resistant shoes.
Contact and collaboration | Constant contact with others (42%); daily face-to-face discussions with individuals and teams (62%); teamwork is important (41% rate it very important); daily telephone communication (46%).
Standing and hand use | Stand more than half the time (36%), walk or run more than half the time (35%), and use hands to handle or control materials and tools more than half the time (34%).
Accuracy and repetition | Exactness or accuracy is important (46% rate it very important); repeating the same tasks is important (47% rate it very important); repetitive motions occur continually or almost continually (17%).
Pace and pressure | Daily time pressure (36%); leading or coordinating others is important (48%).
Decisions and impact | Daily decision-making is relatively uncommon (37% report never making decisions); decisions significantly affect coworkers and company results (38% report important results).
Responsibility and consequences | High responsibility for others' health and safety (25%); serious consequences of error (65% consider them serious).

Environment and pace | 88% of respondents work indoors in controlled environments daily, and 36% face daily time pressure; 36% stand more than half the time and 35% walk more than half the time. These figures are respondent percentages, not measures of every kitchen's peak workload or every individual's working hours. Check actual shifts and workload at the site.

Tools and materials | Equipment: manual and powered slicing and cutting utensils, sanitizing cabinets and dishwashing equipment, refrigerators, freezers and refrigerated cabinets, hot-holding equipment, plates, trays and tableware, scales and measuring utensils, thermometers, and cleaning and sanitizing tools. Materials: ingredients for preparation (produce, meat, seafood and shellfish, salad and sauce ingredients, coffee, tea, and beverage ingredients), disposable gloves, aprons and slip-resistant shoes, cleaning and sanitizing supplies, and packaging and portioning containers. Documents: orders or menus and preparation instructions, food safety and hygiene procedures (including allergen and temperature control), refrigerator and freezer temperature logs, usage records, and equipment fault and reporting procedures. All portion, temperature, and hygiene requirements must follow the procedures and supervisor instructions in effect for the shift.
Check ingredients and orders → Wash and cut → Prepare cold foods and drinks → Portion, plate, and serve → Record temperatures and usage → Clean, sanitize, and hand over

Quality standards | Prepared food must meet orders or instructions and food safety procedures: ingredients must be fresh and within their shelf life, raw and cooked foods separated, utensils and worktops properly cleaned and sanitized, refrigeration and freezing temperatures within procedural limits, and portions and plating compliant. Usage, temperature, and abnormality records must be truthful and traceable. If anything conflicts with food safety procedures, supervisor instructions, or temperature-control requirements, first consult the supervisor or food safety lead and document it. Do not independently continue using suspect ingredients or skip cleaning and sanitizing steps.

Boundaries with adjacent duties | This page covers O*NET-SOC 35-2021.00. Adjacent but distinct occupations include Cooks, Fast Food (heating and cooking food); Fast Food and Counter Workers (taking orders, serving food, and taking payments); Dishwashers (cleaning tableware and kitchens); Butchers and Meat Cutters (breaking down and cutting large pieces of meat); Baristas (preparing espresso drinks and providing counter service); and Waiters and Waitresses (taking orders, delivering dishes, and providing table service). Their processes, utensils, and authorization differ from this occupation. Cooking decisions, cutting and grading, and food safety incident determinations belong to the relevant positions and authorities; workers in this occupation must not replace their judgments or sign-offs.

Boundary review points | Stop and escalate when ingredients are expired, spoiled, have unusual odors or damaged packaging; refrigerator or freezer temperatures exceed procedural limits; allergen contamination or raw-to-cooked cross-contamination is suspected; equipment malfunctions, blades are damaged, or sanitizing equipment fails; hands have wounds or symptoms such as fever or diarrhea occur; or any situation could delay food service or cause a food safety incident. Supervisors, food safety leads, or duty managers handle these situations under company procedures and regulations.
Check ingredients → Wash and cut → Prepare cold foods and drinks → Portion and plate → Record temperatures and usage → Clean, sanitize, and hand over

Difference from cooks-fast-food (fast-food cooks): They heat and cook food and decide cooking doneness and finished output. This occupation mainly involves washing, cutting, preparing cold foods and drinks, and portioning, and usually does not make cooking or heating decisions. The roles differ in authorization for heat processing and responsibility for finished food.

Difference from food-and-beverage-serving-and-related-workers | That link represents the food and beverage serving occupational group, not the individual 35-3023 Fast Food and Counter Workers occupation. Specific ordering, payment, service, or preparation duties must be checked against the relevant constituent occupation.

Difference from dishwashers: Their main duties are washing tableware and utensils and cleaning kitchens. This occupation also washes and cuts ingredients, prepares cold foods and beverages, portions food, and records temperatures and usage, giving it a broader scope of food safety and hygiene responsibility.

Difference from butchers-and-meat-cutters: They break down, cut, grade, and package large pieces of meat, poultry, and fish, using more specialized processes and knife skills. This occupation only cuts and debones as needed for preparation and does not assume responsibility for meat breakdown and grading or specialist retail compliance.

Before choosing this occupation, compare actual task proportions (washing and cutting, cold-food and beverage preparation, portioning and plating, cleaning, and records), qualification and training routes (on-the-job training, food safety and hygiene training, and allergen management training), shifts and physical demands (standing and walking, early and late shifts, weekends and holidays, and peak-time pressure), and progression routes (fast-food cook, barista, butcher or meat cutter, or first-line food preparation and serving supervisor). Restaurants, canteens, hospital and institutional kitchens, and food retail differ considerably; check actual recruitment requirements and site observations.

Responsibility boundaries cannot be inferred from similar job titles. Even within food service, heating and cooking, cold-food preparation, dishwashing, meat cutting, counter beverages, and customer service differ in materials, processes, utensils, and authorization. Moving between roles requires learning the new processes, utensils, and hygiene procedures; judgment and sign-off authority from the former role does not carry over. Food safety incident handling and equipment repairs must be undertaken by the responsible parties.

AI task exposure | Digital tools may assist with order and usage records, inventory and restocking reminders, refrigerator and freezer temperature logs and alerts, hygiene checklists, and scheduling. On-site workers remain responsible for judging ingredient and equipment condition, washing and cutting, preparing cold foods and drinks, portioning and plating, implementing hygiene procedures, and handling abnormalities. Task exposure does not mean job replacement.

Occupational definition | Food preparation workers help kitchens wash and cut ingredients, prepare cold foods and beverages, portion food, assemble plates, record temperatures and usage, store and restock supplies, and clean and sanitize. O*NET's overview mainly concerns preparation other than cooking, but its tasks also include assisting with cooking, hot beverages, dishwashing, and some cashier duties. Distinguish adjacent roles by their main duties rather than absolutely excluding individual processes.

Data and system requirements | Before adoption, check whether usage and temperature records can be traced to original shifts and batches; how equipment fault and maintenance records are defined; version control for orders, menus, and preparation instructions; retention periods for allergen and temperature records; whether paper records can be used when networks or equipment fail; and whether dashboards and checklists use consistent definitions.

Human control points and review | On-site staff, supervisors, or food safety leads must judge ingredient usability, wash, cut and prepare food, measure temperatures and manage storage, implement hygiene and sanitizing procedures, portion and plate, and record and report. Any tool-generated conclusions about temperatures, inventory, inspections, or records require human review before use, with a documented checking trail.

Remaining responsibility | Decisions that must not receive automatic clearance include whether ingredients can be used, refrigeration and freezing temperatures comply, raw and cooked foods are separated, cleaning and sanitizing are complete, food can continue to be served, and items must be withdrawn or discarded. Tool output does not itself constitute an acceptability finding or authorization decision.

Failure risks | Unreviewed tool output may directly lead to expired or spoiled ingredients being used, temperature abnormalities being missed, allergen contamination, inaccurate usage records, or unconfirmed service or withdrawal decisions being implemented as established plans. These can cause food safety incidents and health risks to customers and patients. Before implementation, identify who reviews the output and which original records they use.

Employment evidence boundaries | Employment and wage data for this occupation must be distinguished by statistical scope. U.S. O*NET and BLS figures are estimates under specific definitions and cannot be directly extrapolated to mainland China or other regions. Chinese industry-category average wages are background proxies, not occupational wage findings. All generated content should be traceable to original inputs and sources; fluent wording must not be treated as evidence of correctness.

Practical response | Introduce digital tools first into low-risk steps that can be reversed and audited, such as organizing order and usage records, temperature logs and alerts, inventory and restocking reminders, and hygiene checklists. Follow confirmation by supervisors and food safety leads and actual food service conditions. Decide whether to expand use based on error records and food safety incidents, while always retaining human confirmation of ingredient, temperature, and food-service judgments.

Cross-market statistical boundaries | Mainland China and the United States use different industry and occupational classifications. Mainland China publishes average wages of urban-unit employees by national economic industry category, without separately reporting this occupation; the United States provides estimates by SOC occupation and industry. The figures cannot be combined or converted, and industry averages cannot substitute for occupational wages.

Insufficient evidence: This page has not obtained public occupational wage statistics precisely matching Food Preparation Workers. Industry averages, recruitment offers, and third-party estimates are not used to fill the gap.

U.S. wage coverage | OEWS surveys wages of full-time and part-time employees and excludes self-employment. Wages include items such as tips. The median is not a starting wage or a contract offer applicable to any region.

U.S. wage evidence—reference period | Wages come from May 2025 OEWS; employment, growth, and openings come from the 2025—2035 employment projections. These datasets have different reference points and must not be combined into a finding for the same point in time.

U.S. wage evidence—measurement units | Figures are published in dollars per hour and dollars per year. Annual mean wages assume full-time, year-round work. Converting hourly and annual figures does not establish an individual's actual income, which also depends on hours, part-time work, and seasonality.

U.S. coverage | OEWS covers full-time and part-time employees and excludes the self-employed, owners or partners of unincorporated firms, domestic workers, and unpaid family workers. Part-time, seasonal, and hourly workers are not automatically excluded; tips are included in wages.

Occupational scope | This page corresponds to 35-2021. Fast-food cooks 35-2011, chefs 35-1011, fast food and counter workers 35-3023, waiters and waitresses 35-3031, dishwashers 35-9021, and butchers 51-3021 are explained separately. paragraphs: Conclusion | The core distinction between this occupation and adjacent occupations is whether the work concerns raw ingredients, heat processing, tableware, meat cuts, or customer service. This occupation centers on washing and cutting, preparing cold foods and drinks, portioning, and hygiene. Fast-food cooks heat and cook finished foods; fast food and counter workers take orders, serve food, and take payments; dishwashers clean tableware and kitchens; butchers and meat cutters break down and cut large pieces of meat; and baristas prepare espresso drinks and provide counter service. Utensils, processes, and authorization differ; judgment and sign-off authority cannot simply carry over between roles.

Evidence note | The comparisons below draw on O*NET occupational classifications and publicly available materials offered for sale. They help distinguish adjacent occupations' work and suitability of choices, and do not establish qualifications, hiring decisions, or pay. Wages and employment must be checked separately for each occupation's SOC definition. This table makes no numerical comparisons and does not use one occupation's wages as a proxy for another.

Introduction | The comparison uses four columns: career direction, core work and outputs, key differences, and which choices it may suit. These roles often connect through kitchen workflows, but workflow connections do not make them interchangeable. Moving between directions requires learning the relevant processes, utensils, and hygiene procedures.

Centers on food preparation other than cooking: washing and cutting raw ingredients, making cold foods, salads, and beverages, portioning and plating, recording temperatures and usage, and cleaning and sanitizing.

May better suit people willing to follow washing, cutting, and portioning procedures while maintaining hygiene. Those who prefer heating food and creating finished dishes may find an adjacent direction more suitable.

Outputs are foods and ingredients ready for cooking or direct service: ingredient checks, washing and cutting, cold-food and beverage preparation, portioning and plating, temperature and usage records, and cleaning and sanitizing.
This occupation: Food Preparation Workers

Centers on heating and cooking: deciding cooking doneness and finished output and taking responsibility for doneness and taste, usually without auxiliary duties such as cold-food preparation and dishwashing.

May better suit people willing to make heating and doneness judgments and take responsibility for finished food. Those who prefer raw-ingredient handling and hygiene control may prefer this occupation.
Produces hot dishes through ingredient preparation and seasoning, heating and finishing, plating, and food service.
Cooks, Fast Food

Centers on taking orders, serving food, and customer service: interacting with customers, operating the register, and serving orders, usually without responsibility for kitchen preparation or hygiene records.
May better suit people who prefer customer interaction and a front-counter pace. Those who prefer kitchen preparation and procedural work may prefer this occupation.
Outputs are completed orders, food service, and payments: taking orders and communicating preparation needs, serving food and setting tables, and handling payments and settlement.
Fast Food and Counter Workers

Centers on washing tableware and utensils and cleaning kitchens: operating dishwashing equipment and cleaning floors and bins, usually without responsibility for food preparation or temperature records.
May better suit people willing to do cleaning and repetitive physical work with less involvement in food preparation. Those who prefer preparation processes may prefer this occupation.
Produces clean tableware and kitchen environments through utensil washing and sanitizing, floor cleaning and waste removal, and cleaning records.
Dishwashers

Centers on breaking down, cutting, grading, and packaging large pieces of meat, poultry, and fish, using specialized knife and cutting skills and often involving specialist retail and compliance requirements.
May better suit people willing to practice knife, cutting, and grading skills over the long term. Those who only want to cut ingredients for preparation may choose this occupation.
Produces cut and graded meat through breakdown and deboning, cutting and trimming, and weighing, packaging, and labeling.
Butchers and Meat Cutters
Centers on espresso and beverage preparation and counter service: grinding, extraction, milk steaming and latte art, customer interaction, and counter cleaning.
May better suit people who prefer beverage techniques and the pace of counter service. Those who prefer ingredient preparation and hygiene control may prefer this occupation.
Produces beverages and counter service through extraction and milk steaming, beverage preparation and presentation, order-taking and payments, and counter cleaning.
Baristas

Transition | This page compares adjacent roles according to whether they handle raw ingredients, heat processing, tableware, meat cuts, or customer service to help you decide which kind of food-service work you want to pursue over time. In every direction, readiness for work depends on understanding processes, utensils, and food safety procedures, working consistently according to procedures, and passing a practical assessment accepted by the employer or supervisor. Interest questionnaires only help generate questions.

What personalities suit this work? Responsibility, patience, and hygiene awareness matter more than a particular personality type. The O*NET interest code RC (Realistic–Conventional) can provide a starting point for exploration.

Introversion neither rules out exploration nor guarantees fit. O*NET62% report daily face-to-face discussions and 42% constant contact. Observe handovers and abnormality reporting; social intensity cannot be labeled moderate.

What should you prepare before entering? Understand the actual work pace: prolonged standing and walking, peak-time pressure, early and late shifts, weekends, and holidays. Prepare basic food safety and hygiene knowledge. Preparation assistant or cleaning roles can be a starting point.

What are the main pressures? Food safety, allergen, and hygiene errors directly affect others' health (65% in O*NET report serious consequences of error). Peak periods also bring pressure to produce food on time (36% report daily time pressure).

Are there physical requirements? Workers need to stand and walk for long periods, move ingredients and utensils, and use knives and cutting tools. Employment, medical examination, and health-certificate requirements depend on employers and local regulations; this page provides no medical assessment.

BLS typically identifies no formal education, no related experience, and short-term on-the-job training for this exact occupation. O*NET Job Zone1–2 is a grouping and does not establish a universal upper-secondary requirement. Check actual job conditions separately.

Can long-term work harm the body? Cuts from knives and slicers, slips on wet floors, burns from hot drinks, foods, and equipment surfaces, prolonged standing, and repetitive motions are practical costs. Use protective equipment, take breaks, and follow procedures.

Career development and transitions? Workers may progress from preparation assistance to skilled preparation and team leadership, or move into adjacent roles such as fast-food cook, barista, dishwasher, butcher or meat cutter, and first-line food preparation and serving supervisor. Changing directions requires learning new processes and utensils.

Typical U.S. training differs from Chinese entry requirements. Article 44 of China's Food Safety Law requires food safety knowledge training for enterprise employees. Article 45 requires annual health examinations and certification for workers handling ready-to-eat food; this must not be extended to every role.

It does not constitute legal, safety, food safety, hygiene, medical, or contractual advice. Food safety incidents, personal injuries, equipment accidents, and contract disputes must be handled by employers, food safety leads, and the relevant authorities under regulations and contracts.

Direct answer | Occupational risk extends beyond cutting vegetables to three types of failure with serious consequences: food safety and hygiene control failures (expired or spoiled ingredients, temperatures beyond limits, raw/cooked cross-contamination, and allergen contamination); inadequate operational safety controls (cuts from knives, slicers and grinders, slips on wet floors, and burns from hot drinks, foods and equipment surfaces); and record and handover errors (inaccurate usage, temperature and cleaning records preventing identification and traceability).

Evidence scope | O*NET tasks and context support preparation, recordkeeping, hygiene, and collaboration requirements. Failure scenarios are editorial extrapolations, not accident rates. Preparation and receiving workers; businesses, customers, and patients

Expired or spoiled ingredients or those with damaged packaging are used, or refrigerator and freezer temperatures beyond limits go undetected. Food safety incidents and health risks to customers and patients may lead to closures and recalls

Check shelf life and packaging at receiving and storage, store at required temperatures, and measure and record regularly. Immediately isolate, stop using, and report spoiled ingredients or temperatures beyond limits

Raw and cooked foods are not separated, utensils and worktops are not sanitized, or allergens contaminate food. Cross-contamination and allergic reaction risks affect safe food service

Separate raw and cooked foods and allergens under current procedures. Suspected contamination requires isolation, withdrawal from use, and reporting, with disposal decisions made by authorized staff. Suspicion alone does not automatically grant discard authority.
Scenario | Raw meat and ready-to-eat cold foods share a chopping board and knives, and preparation continues without procedural sanitizing.
Preparation workers; businesses
Improper use of cutting, slicing, and grinding utensils or damaged utensils creates risks of cuts, broken blades, and foreign objects

Use knives, hand guards, and slicers according to procedures and immediately withdraw damaged utensils. Keep knives sharp and worktops slip-resistant; handle waste and foreign objects under procedures
Scenario | Using a chipped knife or cutting without required hand protection creates a laceration risk.
Preparation workers and others; businesses and customers
Wet floors or improper handling of hot drinks, foods, equipment surfaces, or cleaning chemicals causes injuries such as slips, burns, and chemical burns
Promptly clear spills and water from floors. Wear slip-resistant shoes and heat-resistant and protective equipment. Dilute, use, and label cleaning chemicals according to procedures
Scenario | Water on the floor is not cleaned promptly, and a worker slips while carrying hot soup and is burned.

Missing or inconsistent usage, temperature, cleaning, and abnormality records break traceability, preventing problem identification and expanding the affected scope

Record usage, refrigerator and freezer temperatures, cleaning, and abnormalities under the shift's procedures; check retained samples against batch numbers. Immediately isolate and report record or label errors

Preparation and support workers; businesses
Prolonged standing and walking, repetitive cutting and washing, and rushing peak-period orders cause musculoskeletal strain and fatigue-related errors
Rotate roles and take work breaks, use slip-resistant and protective equipment, organize work by shift, and promptly report unusual discomfort

entries.answer: Under O*NET-SOC 35-2021.00, workers perform various food preparation duties other than cooking, such as preparing cold foods and shellfish, slicing meat, and brewing coffee or tea. Duties include checking ingredients and shelf life; washing, peeling, slicing, and cutting while separating raw and cooked foods; preparing cold foods, salads, sauces, and drinks to order or instruction; portioning, packaging, plating, and distributing according to menus; measuring and recording food, refrigerator and freezer temperatures and ingredient usage; and cleaning and sanitizing work areas, utensils, and tableware and disposing of waste. Excluded are cooking and heating, recipe and dish decisions, food ingredient and mixing equipment operation, cooking-equipment parameter control, dedicated dishwashing, and general cleaning unrelated to food service.
entries.question: What exactly does this occupation do?

entries.answer: Fast-food cooks heat and cook food and decide doneness and finished output; dishwashers mainly wash tableware and utensils and clean kitchens; butchers and meat cutters break down, cut, and grade meat, poultry, and fish; fast food and counter workers take orders, serve food, and take payments; and baristas prepare espresso drinks and provide counter service. This occupation centers on washing and cutting, preparing cold foods and drinks, portioning and plating, and recording temperatures and usage. Its authorization and outputs differ from those roles.

facts.display_value: Performs various food preparation duties other than cooking, such as preparing cold foods and shellfish, slicing meat, and brewing coffee or tea. Checks ingredients and orders, washes and cuts, prepares cold foods, salads, and beverages as instructed, portions and plates, measures and records temperatures and usage, and cleans and sanitizes while maintaining hygiene, producing foods and ingredients ready for cooking or direct service. Excludes cooking and heating, recipe and dish decisions, food ingredient and mixing equipment operation, cooking-equipment parameter control, dedicated dishwashing, and general cleaning unrelated to food service.
